title: Human Nutrition & Balanced Diet
description: The seven food groups and their roles, balanced diets and changing energy needs, deficiency diseases such as scurvy and rickets, and the laboratory tests for sugars, starch, protein, and fat.

notes.heading: The Seven Food Groups
notes.body: A balanced diet contains seven components, each with a different job in the body. (1) Carbohydrates — the main source of energy; found in bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, and sugar. (2) Proteins — needed for growth and repair of tissues; found in meat, fish, eggs, beans, and nuts. (3) Fats (lipids) — a concentrated energy store, insulation, and protection for organs; found in oils, butter, cheese, and oily fish. (4) Vitamins — needed in tiny amounts to keep body processes working; found in fruit and vegetables. (5) Minerals — also needed in small amounts for specific jobs, e.g. iron for blood and calcium for bones; found in dairy products, red meat, and green vegetables. (6) Fibre (roughage) — indigestible plant material that keeps food moving through the gut and prevents constipation; found in wholegrains, fruit, and vegetables. (7) Water — the solvent for all body chemistry, needed for blood plasma, sweat, and every cell reaction. Only carbohydrates, proteins, and fats supply energy; vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water are essential despite providing none.

notes.heading: Carbohydrates, Proteins and Fats in Detail
notes.body: These three groups are the macronutrients — the parts of the diet needed in large amounts. Carbohydrates are made of sugar units; starch is a long chain of glucose and is the main storage carbohydrate in plants, while glycogen is the storage form in animals. During digestion, starch is broken down to glucose, which cells then use in respiration to release energy. Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Besides growth and repair, they form enzymes, antibodies, and much of muscle; the body can store neither protein nor amino acids, so a regular supply is needed. Fats are made of fatty acids and glycerol. Gram for gram they release about twice as much energy as carbohydrates, making them a compact energy store; fat under the skin also insulates against heat loss, and some vitamins (A, D, E, K) are fat-soluble. Too much of any energy nutrient is stored as fat, which is why energy intake should match energy use.

notes.heading: Vitamins and Minerals
notes.body: Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients — required only in small quantities, but essential for health. Key vitamins: vitamin C keeps skin and gums healthy and helps wounds heal; sources include citrus fruits, berries, and peppers. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones; sources include oily fish, eggs, and sunlight acting on the skin. Vitamin A is needed for good vision, especially in dim light; sources include carrots and liver. Key minerals: iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen; sources include red meat, spinach, and lentils. Calcium builds and maintains bones and teeth and helps muscles contract; sources include milk, cheese, and leafy greens. Iodine is needed by the thyroid gland to make hormones that control metabolic rate. Because the body cannot make most vitamins and minerals itself, they must come from food — which is why a varied diet matters.

notes.heading: Deficiency Diseases
notes.body: A deficiency disease develops when the diet lacks a particular vitamin or mineral over a long period. Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C: symptoms include bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and tiredness. It famously affected sailors on long voyages without fresh fruit, and is prevented by eating citrus fruit and vegetables. Rickets is caused by lack of vitamin D (or calcium): bones stay soft and bend, causing bowed legs in children; prevented by vitamin D from oily fish, fortified foods, and sunlight. Anaemia is caused by lack of iron: with too little haemoglobin, the blood carries less oxygen, causing tiredness, weakness, and pale skin; prevented by eating iron-rich foods such as red meat and green vegetables. Goitre, a swollen thyroid gland, results from iodine deficiency. The key pattern to remember: each deficiency produces specific symptoms, and each is cured or prevented simply by restoring the missing nutrient — proof of how precisely the body depends on tiny amounts of these substances.

notes.heading: Balanced Diet and Energy Needs
notes.body: A balanced diet provides all seven food groups in the right proportions, with enough energy to match the body's needs but not so much that the excess is stored as fat. Energy is measured in kilojoules (kJ). Energy needs vary between people: they increase with body size, with physical activity (athletes and manual workers need far more), during growth spurts in teenagers, and during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Males generally need more energy than females of the same age because of greater average muscle mass, and needs fall in old age as activity and muscle decline. Eating too little energy or protein causes weight loss and, in severe cases, deficiency diseases such as kwashiorkor (protein deficiency). Eating too much causes obesity, which raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and joint problems. Guide models such as the eatwell plate show the proportions: plenty of fruit, vegetables, and starchy carbohydrates; some protein and dairy; and only small amounts of fatty and sugary foods.

notes.heading: Food Tests in the Laboratory
notes.body: Four standard tests identify the main nutrients in a food sample. Starch test: add a few drops of brown iodine solution — it turns blue-black if starch is present. Reducing sugar test (e.g. glucose): add Benedict's solution and HEAT in a water bath — the blue solution changes through green and yellow to brick-red (orange-red) if sugar is present; the more sugar, the further the colour moves along that sequence. Protein test: add Biuret reagent (dilute sodium hydroxide then copper sulfate solution) — it changes from blue to purple (violet) if protein is present; no heating needed. Fat test (ethanol emulsion test): shake the food with ethanol, then pour the ethanol into water — a cloudy white emulsion forms if fat is present, because the fat dissolved in the ethanol comes out of solution as tiny droplets. Learn each test as reagent + conditions + positive colour. A control using distilled water shows the negative result for comparison. These tests are qualitative — they show which nutrient is present, not exactly how much.

notes.heading: From Food to Fuel: The Digestion Link
notes.body: Most food molecules are too large to pass from the gut into the blood, so they must first be digested — broken down into small, soluble molecules. (Digestion is covered fully in its own topic; this is the nutrition-side summary.) Carbohydrase enzymes break starch down into glucose; protease enzymes break proteins down into amino acids; lipase enzymes break fats down into fatty acids and glycerol. Most digestion happens in the small intestine, and the small soluble products are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine into the blood, which carries them to every cell. Cells use glucose in respiration to release energy, use amino acids to build their own proteins, and store surplus energy as fat. Fibre is the exception: it is never digested or absorbed, passing through the gut while absorbing water and giving the gut muscles something to push against. Water, vitamins, and minerals are small enough to be absorbed without digestion. This is why the diet must supply all seven groups — each one feeds a different step in keeping cells alive, repaired, and energised.

flashcards.definition: The body's main energy source, made of sugar units; includes starch and sugars.
flashcards.example: Bread, rice, pasta, and potatoes are rich in starch.

flashcards.definition: Nutrient needed for growth and repair, built from amino acids; also forms enzymes and antibodies.
flashcards.example: Meat, fish, eggs, and beans are protein-rich foods.

flashcards.definition: Concentrated energy store that also insulates the body and protects organs; made of fatty acids and glycerol.
flashcards.example: Butter, oils, and cheese are high in fat.

flashcards.definition: Vitamin needed for healthy skin and gums and wound healing; deficiency causes scurvy.
flashcards.example: Found in citrus fruits such as oranges and lemons.

flashcards.definition: Vitamin that helps absorb calcium for strong bones; deficiency causes rickets.
flashcards.example: Made in skin exposed to sunlight; also found in oily fish.

flashcards.definition: Mineral needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells; deficiency causes anaemia.
flashcards.example: Red meat, spinach, and lentils are good sources.

flashcards.definition: Indigestible plant material that keeps food moving through the gut and prevents constipation.
flashcards.example: Wholemeal bread, fruit, and vegetables supply fibre.

flashcards.definition: A diet containing all seven food groups in the right proportions, with energy intake matching energy use.
flashcards.example: Plenty of fruit and vegetables, some protein and dairy, little fatty or sugary food.

flashcards.definition: Brown iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present.
flashcards.example: A potato slice turns blue-black with iodine.

flashcards.definition: Heat the sample with blue Benedict's solution; reducing sugar turns it green, yellow, then brick-red.
flashcards.example: Glucose solution turns brick-red when heated with Benedict's.

flashcards.definition: Biuret reagent changes from blue to purple when protein is present; no heating is needed.
flashcards.example: Egg albumen gives a purple colour with Biuret reagent.

flashcards.definition: Shake the sample with ethanol, then add to water; a cloudy white emulsion shows fat is present.
flashcards.example: Oil shaken with ethanol and poured into water turns the water milky white.

questions.stem: Which food group is the body's main source of energy?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates such as starch and glucose are the main energy source. Proteins are mainly for growth and repair, while vitamins and minerals provide no energy at all.

questions.stem: What is the main role of protein in the diet?
choices: Keeping food moving through the gut
Acting as a solvent for cell reactions
questions.explanation: Protein supplies amino acids for building and repairing cells. Insulation is a role of fat, gut movement is fibre's job, and water is the body's solvent.

questions.stem: Which nutrient is added to a sample tested with iodine solution, and what is a positive result?
questions.explanation: Iodine tests for starch, turning from brown to blue-black. Brick-red is Benedict's (sugar), purple is Biuret (protein), and the white emulsion is the fat test.

questions.stem: A sailor on a long voyage develops bleeding gums and wounds that heal slowly. Which deficiency disease is this, and which nutrient is missing?
questions.explanation: Bleeding gums and poor healing are classic symptoms of scurvy, caused by lack of vitamin C from fresh fruit and vegetables.

questions.stem: Which two nutrients provide energy but are NOT carbohydrates?
questions.explanation: Only carbohydrates, proteins, and fats supply energy. Vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water are essential for health but release no energy.

questions.stem: Why does a 16-year-old athlete need more energy from food than an elderly person?
choices: Young, active, growing bodies use more energy for movement and growth
Athletes need more vitamins, which provide energy
questions.explanation: Energy needs rise with physical activity and growth, both of which are high in a teenage athlete, and fall with age as activity and muscle mass decline. Vitamins never provide energy.

questions.stem: A food sample is shaken with ethanol and the ethanol is poured into water, giving a cloudy white mixture. Which nutrient has been detected?
questions.explanation: This is the ethanol emulsion test: fat dissolved in the ethanol comes out of solution in water as tiny droplets, forming a milky emulsion.

questions.stem: In the Benedict's test, why is the mixture heated in a water bath rather than left at room temperature?
choices: Heating is required for the colour change with reducing sugars to occur
Heating kills bacteria in the food
Heating turns the sugar into starch
questions.explanation: Benedict's reagent only reacts with reducing sugars when heated, progressing blue → green → yellow → brick-red. Without heat, no colour change occurs.

questions.stem: A child has soft, bowed leg bones. Which nutrient is most likely lacking, and what is the condition called?
questions.explanation: Soft, bending bones are the hallmark of rickets, caused by lack of vitamin D (or calcium), which is needed to harden bone with calcium.

questions.stem: A patient is tired, weak, and pale, and a blood test shows too little haemoglobin. Which mineral should their diet include more of?
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin contains iron, so iron deficiency causes anaemia — exactly these symptoms. Calcium affects bones and iodine affects the thyroid.

questions.stem: Why must starch be digested before it can enter the blood, while water does not?
choices: Starch is a large insoluble molecule that must be broken into small soluble glucose molecules; water is already small enough to absorb
Water is digested by enzymes in the stomach instead
Starch contains more energy than water
The blood can only carry protein molecules
questions.explanation: Only small, soluble molecules can pass through the gut wall into the blood. Starch molecules are far too large, so carbohydrase enzymes break them down to glucose; water, vitamins, and minerals need no digestion.

questions.stem: A student tests four food samples and records: A turns iodine blue-black; B turns purple with Biuret; C turns brick-red with heated Benedict's; D gives a cloudy emulsion with ethanol and water. Which row correctly identifies the nutrients?
choices: A protein, B starch, C fat, D sugar
A starch, B protein, C reducing sugar, D fat
A sugar, B fat, C starch, D protein
A fat, B sugar, C protein, D starch
questions.explanation: Match each test to its positive result: iodine → starch (blue-black), Biuret → protein (purple), heated Benedict's → reducing sugar (brick-red), ethanol emulsion → fat (cloudy white).

questions.stem: Two people eat identical diets, but one works in an office and the other is a builder. Over months, the office worker gains weight while the builder does not. What is the best explanation?
choices: The builder's body destroys the extra nutrients instead of storing them
The office worker's gut absorbs more of the food than the builder's
The builder's greater activity uses up the energy that the office worker stores as fat
Office work converts carbohydrate into protein
questions.explanation: A balanced diet must match energy intake to energy use. The builder expends far more energy through physical work, while the office worker's surplus energy is stored as fat.

questions.stem: A sample turns blue-black with iodine AND brick-red with heated Benedict's solution. What does this tell you, and why might this surprise someone who tested the same food before it was cooked?
choices: The food contains only starch; cooking makes no difference
The food contains starch and reducing sugar; cooking can break some starch down into sugars, so raw food might not have tested positive for sugar
The tests are unreliable and should be repeated
The food contains fat and protein, not carbohydrate
questions.explanation: Both carbohydrate tests are positive. Cooking partially breaks starch into smaller sugars, so the cooked sample can test positive for reducing sugar even if the raw food did not.

questions.stem: Which statement about fibre and water is correct?
choices: Both are digested by enzymes to release energy
Fibre prevents constipation by adding bulk, and water acts as a solvent for body chemistry — neither provides energy
Fibre is absorbed into the blood, while water is not
Both are stored as fat if eaten in excess
questions.explanation: Fibre is never digested — it adds bulk that keeps the gut moving — and water is the solvent for blood and cell reactions. Neither is an energy nutrient, and neither can be stored as fat.
